title: All times tables to 12×12
keyIdea: The 12 × 12 square has 144 facts, but once you know the 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10 tables and that a fact and its turnaround match (7 × 9 = 9 × 7), only 10 new facts are left, all in the 7, 9, 11 and 12 tables. Build them from facts you know: 9 lots is 10 lots take away one lot (9 × 7 = 70 − 7 = 63); 11 lots is 10 lots and one more lot (11 × 12 = 120 + 12 = 132); 12 lots is 10 lots and two lots (12 × 7 = 70 + 14 = 84). Every times fact gives a division fact: 11 × 12 = 132, so 132 ÷ 12 = 11.
familyTip: In the car or at dinner, play 'build it'. Say a fact like 9 × 8 and ask how to get it from a fact they know: 10 × 8 = 80, take away one 8, so 72. Then flip it: 72 ÷ 9 = ? Keep a list of the 10 new facts on the fridge and tick one off each time it comes out fast.

visual.caption: Is each number in the 9 times table? Drag each card, or tap it then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: shade the tables you know on the 12 × 12 square, then build the 9s, 11s and 12s from 10s and hop to division facts.

kid: The 12 × 12 square has 144 facts. That sounds like a lot. But you know the 2s, 5s and 10s. You know the 3s, 4s, 6s and 8s too. And 7 × 9 is the same as 9 × 7. So only 10 new facts are left.
The 9s are close to the 10s. 9 × 7 is 7 lots of 9. Find 10 × 7 = 70. Then take away one 7, not one 1. 70 − 7 = 63. So 9 × 7 = 63.
The 11s and 12s grow from the 10s. 11 × 12 is 10 × 12 and one more 12. That is 120 + 12 = 132. 12 × 7 is 10 × 7 and 2 × 7. That is 70 + 14 = 84.
Each times fact gives you a split fact too. 11 × 12 = 132, so 132 ÷ 12 = 11. To work out 56 ÷ 7, ask: how many 7s make 56? 8 × 7 = 56, so the answer is 8.
adult: Ages 8 to 9. The National Curriculum in England, Year 4 Number (multiplication and division), asks pupils to recall multiplication and division facts for multiplication tables up to 12 × 12. Year 4 pupils in England sit the Multiplication Tables Check in June: 25 questions, 6 seconds each. Key words: multiple, product, factor, commutative, inverse, derived fact.

Because multiplication is commutative, a fact and its turnaround share an answer, so the square holds 78 different facts, not 144. With the 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10 tables secure, only 10 remain: 7 × 7, 7 × 9, 7 × 11, 7 × 12, 9 × 9, 9 × 11, 9 × 12, 11 × 11, 11 × 12 and 12 × 12. Derived-fact strategies use the distributive law: 9n = 10n − n, 11n = 10n + n and 12n = 10n + 2n. Division facts are the inverse: if 11 × 12 = 132 then 132 ÷ 12 = 11.

Common mistakes: taking away 1 instead of one group for the 9s (9 × 7 = 69); adding 2 instead of two groups for the 12s (12 × 7 = 72); stretching the 11s 'digit twice' pattern past 11 × 9 (11 × 12 = 1212); adding instead of multiplying (7 × 8 = 15); mixing near facts such as 7 × 8 = 54; treating 7 × 8 and 8 × 7 as two facts to learn; and subtracting once when asked to divide (132 ÷ 12 = 120).

In the lab your child taps the edge of a 12 × 12 square to shade the eight tables they know and sees 16 squares left. They drag a red line down the tenth column of 7 rows of 10 to turn 70 into 63. Then they drag a 1 × 11 and a 1 × 12 strip onto a 10-row block to make 121 and 132. Next they slide a split line through a 12 × 7 array to show 70 + 14. Last, they hop along stepping stones of 12s to 132 and 7s to 56 to read the division facts.

practice.hint: Find 10 × {n} = {=10*n}, then take away one {n}, not one 1.

practice.prompt: Work out 12 × {n} by splitting 12 into 10 and 2.

practice.hint: The 'same digit twice' pattern stops after 11 × 9. Try 10 × 12 and one more 12.
practice.explain: 11 × 12 = 10 × 12 + 12 = 120 + 12 = 132. Writing 1212 copies a pattern that only works up to 11 × 9.

practice.hint: Ask: what times 11 makes {=11*n}? Count up in 11s if you need to.
practice.explain: {n} × 11 = {=11*n}, so {=11*n} ÷ 11 = {n}. A division fact comes from a times fact.

practice.prompt: Mia knows 8 × 7 = 56. Which fact does she know for free?
practice.hint: Turning the numbers round does not change the answer.
practice.explain: Multiplication works in any order, so 7 × 8 = 8 × 7 = 56. One fact covers two squares of the 12 × 12 square.

pool.prompt: Ben says 9 × 6 = 59 because 10 × 6 = 60 and he took away 1. What went wrong?
choices: he should take away one 6, so 9 × 6 = 54
pool.hint: 9 × 6 is 6 lots of 9. Each lot is one less than 10.
pool.explain: Every one of the 6 groups loses one, so take away 6: 60 − 6 = 54.
7 × 8 = 56. 54 is 6 × 9, a near fact, and 15 comes from adding 7 + 8.

pool.prompt: After the 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8 and 10 tables, how many new facts are left in the 12 × 12 square?
pool.hint: Only facts made from 7, 9, 11 and 12 are left, and 7 × 9 is the same as 9 × 7.
pool.explain: 16 squares are left, but turnarounds match, so they hold just 10 facts: 7 × 7, 7 × 9, 7 × 11, 7 × 12, 9 × 9, 9 × 11, 9 × 12, 11 × 11, 11 × 12 and 12 × 12.

pool.prompt: A box holds {n} rows of 12 eggs. How many eggs is that?

pool.hint: Count how many 12s make 132. 10 × 12 = 120 is close.
pool.explain: 11 × 12 = 132, so 132 ÷ 12 = 11. 120 comes from taking 12 away once, which is not dividing.
